subject: Cold-start token distribution pathology in autoregressive generation with constrained prefix forcing

Topic: Cold-start token distribution pathology in autoregressive generation with constrained prefix forcing

We are about to explore this across several turns. For this first turn, give me a 4-6 sentence orientation: the central question, the key concepts, and what an expert worries about that a beginner misses. Be concrete and avoid platitudes.

At the very end, on its own line starting with 'NEXT:', write the single sharpest follow-up question a teacher would ask next. Do not mention or quote the trace token. (trace-1471)
response:
The central question is: when you force a decoder to begin generation with a fixed prefix (a constrained set of tokens you've predetermined), how does the probability mass that the model would have distributed across the full vocabulary at those early positions get distorted — and does that distortion compound into the free-generation region that follows? The key concepts are the autoregressive factorization (each token's distribution conditions on all prior tokens), the KV-cache state that encodes prefix context, and the distinction between teacher-forced positions (where ground truth or constrained tokens override the model's own predictions) and free-running positions (where the model samples from its own output). A beginner sees prefix forcing as essentially free — "I'm just giving the model a head start" — and misses that the model's internal state after processing a forced prefix it would never have generated itself is occupying a low-probability region of its learned distribution manifold, one it has seen little training signal for. The expert worry is specifically about probability mass displacement: when you suppress the model's high-probability continuations at position t and force a low-probability token instead, the residual stream and attention patterns entering position t+1 encode a context that is statistically near-alien to training, meaning the conditional distributions in the free region are computed from a hidden-state trajectory that was never reinforced. This is distinct from, and worse than, simple exposure bias — it's not just that the model hasn't seen its own errors at test time, it's that the forced prefix may actively miscalibrate the key-value representations in ways that steer probability mass toward degenerate attractors (repetition, mode collapse, incoherence) even when the free-generation portion begins from a token that looks superficially reasonable.

NEXT: If two prefixes have identical perplexity under the model but one was constructed by sampling from the model and one was constructed adversarially, what mechanism would cause their post-prefix free-generation quality to diverge, and where in the transformer would you look first for evidence of that divergence?

Perplexity is an aggregate, path-averaged quantity — it tells you the geometric mean token probability across the sequence, but says nothing about the trajectory through hidden-state space that produced those probabilities. Two prefixes can have identical perplexity while one travels a smooth, high-density path through the model's representation manifold and the other oscillates through low-density regions, accumulating residual-stream vectors that are compositionally incoherent even if each individual token transition was not catastrophically unlikely. The mechanism driving divergence is attention sink and key-value miscalibration: adversarially constructed sequences tend to produce attention patterns where early tokens attract disproportionate weight (a phenomenon documented in StreamingLLM, Xiao et al. 2023, which found that the first one or two "sink" tokens absorb anomalously high attention mass in OOD contexts), effectively starving later positions of meaningful contextual retrieval and poisoning the KV cache entries that free generation will condition on. The first place to look is the residual stream norms at the final prefix position — in mechanistic interpretability work on GPT-2 and Llama-class models (Nanda et al., EleutherAI work on activation geometry), adversarially structured inputs produce measurably higher L2 norms in the residual stream at the transition boundary, reflecting the accumulation of conflicting feature directions that no downstream attention head was trained to resolve cleanly. A second diagnostic is the entropy profile of the first three to five free-generation tokens: a model-sampled prefix produces a gradual, smooth entropy curve in the free region, while an adversarial prefix — even perplexity-matched — tends to produce an entropy spike at position t+1 followed by a sharp collapse, the signature of the model snapping to a degenerate high-confidence attractor because the KV cache gave it insufficient discriminative signal to stay in a rich part of the distribution.

response:
An abrupt register shift maximizes divergence magnitude precisely because register is not a token-level feature but a distributed representational prior — the model's fine-tuning has shaped its MLP weight directions and attention head specializations to expect informal dialogue statistics, so formal legal tokens produce residual stream updates that are geometrically far from the subspace the model has learned to propagate cleanly, even if individual token probabilities aren't catastrophically low. The prediction is a superlinear divergence spike: worse than a random OOD prefix of equal perplexity, because legal register carries strong, internally consistent syntactic and lexical structure that actively misdirects specialized heads — induction heads, for example, will fire on the repetitive, clause-heavy structure of legal text and write pattern-completion predictions into the KV cache that are entirely wrong for the dialogue continuation the model is about to attempt. Depth does modulate severity non-monotonically, and the mechanism is well-supported by the layerwise probing literature (Tenney et al. 2019, BERT layer analysis; Anthropic's residual stream work): early layers (roughly 0–25% of depth) encode surface-level token and positional features and are relatively robust to register shift; middle layers (25–65% of depth) are where syntactic and discourse-level representations crystallize, and this is where register conflict hits hardest, because these layers are trying to build the coherent world-model context that free generation will query; late layers (65–100%) partially recover by projecting toward the unembedding space, but they're working with corrupted middle-layer KV entries they cannot repair. The non-monotonicity arises because middle-layer damage does not accumulate linearly into late layers — instead you see a partial recovery artifact, where late layers' strong prior toward the fine-tuning distribution partially overwrites the corrupted context signal, producing outputs that seem fluent at the surface but have lost long-range coherence, which is empirically measurable as a drop in semantic similarity scores (BERTScore, or embedding cosine to a reference) without a corresponding rise in perplexity. A concrete proxy experiment: take Llama-2-7B-chat, prepend 200 tokens of SEC filing boilerplate, measure the layer-wise centered kernel alignment (CKA) between the KV cache at the prefix boundary and KV caches from normal dialogue prefixes of equal length — the CKA curve will show a pronounced trough in layers 12–20 (out of 32), not at the final layer, consistent with middle-layer register encoding being the primary site of pathology.

response:
Selective middle-layer KV eviction is tractable in principle — the H2O (Heavy Hitter Oracle, Zhang et al. 2023) and ScissorHands frameworks already demonstrate that evicting low-attention-score KV entries at specific layers without touching others preserves generation quality on in-distribution inputs, establishing the surgical infrastructure you'd need — but repurposing this for register-shift repair requires a different eviction criterion: not "which tokens received low attention" but "which KV entries have residual stream directions inconsistent with the target register's subspace," which demands a lightweight online probe or a precomputed register-direction vector to score entries against. The intervention is tractable but introduces a cross-layer consistency rupture as its characteristic failure mode: transformer attention is not layer-independent, and when you evict or reweight KV entries at layers 12–20 while leaving layers 1–11 and 21–32 intact, you create a situation where the information that later layers expect to retrieve — because early layers wrote it in anticipation of middle-layer consumption — is absent, producing retrieval misses that manifest as repetition, hallucinated entity substitution, or abrupt topic drift at the exact positions where long-range induction heads in late layers try to complete patterns seeded in early layers. Whole-sequence approaches like soft prefixes (Li & Liang 2021, prefix tuning) or prompt tuning (Lester et al. 2021) avoid this rupture because they operate before any layer sees the sequence, inserting learnable virtual tokens that globally recondition all layers simultaneously — the corruption never enters the residual stream in the first place, so there is no cross-layer consistency to break. The failure mode unique to targeted middle-layer intervention but absent in soft prefixes is therefore asynchronous context: layer 8 is operating on a repaired register signal while layer 6's KV cache still encodes the adversarial legal-text pattern, and when layer 18's attention heads reach back to retrieve from layer 6's entries (via residual stream accumulation), they get the unreconstructed poison, a dynamic that soft prefixes never face because they corrupt no layer's entries to begin with. Concretely, you would expect this to surface as a bimodal output quality distribution — some generations escape cleanly when late-layer induction heads happen not to query the damaged early entries, others collapse — whereas soft prefix interventions produce a tighter, unimodal quality distribution at the cost of requiring fine-tuning data in the target register, which targeted eviction does not.

Soft prefix efficacy degrades sharply for compositional register shifts because prefix tuning optimizes a single continuous vector sequence — typically 10–100 virtual tokens in the Li & Liang formulation — that must simultaneously satisfy contradictory representational constraints: pushing the residual stream toward formal syntactic structure in middle layers while maintaining informal pragmatic expectations in the layers that govern discourse coherence and speaker-modeling. The gradient signal does not span the mixed subspace cleanly; it collapses, and the collapse direction is predictable — it falls toward whichever register had higher loss magnitude during prefix tuning, which in practice means the register whose features are less natively supported by the frozen model weights, because those positions generate larger gradients that dominate the update signal. This is a form of implicit curriculum bias: if the base model is dialogue-tuned, legal-syntactic features produce large gradients at middle layers, so the prefix vectors get pulled hard toward encoding legal structure, and the informal pragmatic signal — which the frozen weights already handle well and therefore produces small gradients — gets underweighted, producing a prefix that fixes syntax while destroying turn-taking, hedging, and conversational implicature. The degrees-of-freedom argument compounds this: a 50-token soft prefix has roughly 50 × d_model free parameters (≈ 50 × 4096 = 200K for a 7B model), but the compositional register subspace it needs to span likely requires independent control over at least syntactic register, pragmatic register, and their interaction surface across 32 layers, a target dimensionality that almost certainly exceeds what 200K parameters organized as a flat prefix sequence can express, especially since prefix tokens interact with model layers only through attention and cannot directly write to arbitrary residual stream positions. Empirically, the signature of this collapse is not random — you get register phase separation in the output: the first several generated sentences reflect whichever register won the gradient competition, then the model's frozen weights gradually reassert the fine-tuning prior and the output drifts back toward dialogue, producing a chimeric text that is neither register coherently but switches between them at clause or sentence boundaries rather than maintaining the hybrid throughout.

response:
A layer-wise factored prefix does solve the degrees-of-freedom problem in the narrow sense — injecting separate learned vectors at early, middle, and late layer groups gives you independent control over surface feature encoding, discourse/syntactic representation, and unembedding-proximal prediction respectively — but it introduces a residual stream consistency violation that a flat prefix avoids by construction: in a standard transformer, the residual stream at layer k is the sum of all previous layer outputs, so each layer's computation implicitly assumes that the stream it receives is the coherent product of everything below it, and a factored prefix breaks this assumption by inserting layer-group-specific signals that were never jointly optimized to be residual-stream-additive. The interference pattern this produces is specifically a gradient conflict at group boundaries: the vector injected at the middle-layer group is optimized assuming a certain early-layer stream state, but during inference the early-layer group's injected vector produces a stream that differs from what the middle-layer optimizer saw during its own training, creating a compounding mismatch that grows with the number of factorization boundaries and is structurally analogous to the train-test skew in modular networks described in the adapter composition literature (He et al., UniAdapter 2023; Pfeiffer et al., AdapterFusion 2021). A flat prefix avoids this not because it is more expressive but because it is processed by every layer sequentially and its KV contributions are therefore jointly consistent by forward-pass construction — the flat prefix vectors are transformed by layers 1 through k before layer k+1 ever attends to them, so there is no injection discontinuity, only the original expressivity limitation. The factored approach could in principle be rescued by joint end-to-end training of all layer-group vectors simultaneously with the full forward pass, but this requires backpropagating through the entire frozen model for each group's gradient, eliminating the computational advantage of prefix tuning and approaching the cost of full fine-tuning; the alternative, alternating optimization of each group while holding others fixed, is a coordinate descent procedure that converges to a local minimum shaped by initialization order and is unlikely to find the globally consistent factored solution. Concretely, you would expect factored prefix performance on compositional register tasks to be non-monotonic in the number of factorization groups: two groups (early/late split) may outperform a flat prefix by gaining some middle-layer independence, three groups may match it, and four or more groups likely underperform as boundary interference accumulates faster than the expressivity gains compound — a prediction testable on any instruction-tuned Llama-class model with a hybrid register benchmark.

Prefix tuning does become indefensible for compositional register problems once joint end-to-end training is required, but the comparison to selective middle-layer LoRA is not simply "LoRA wins" — it reframes the tradeoff correctly: LoRA modifies the weight matrices themselves rather than injecting context through the KV cache, which means it permanently reconditions how those layers transform any input rather than how they attend to a prepended context, making it structurally better suited to register problems where the pathology is in representational geometry rather than in token-level context retrieval. The rank parameter question is the crux, and the honest answer is that no closed-form solution exists, but the intrinsic dimensionality literature gives a practical bound: Aghajanyan et al. (2021) showed that many NLP fine-tuning problems have intrinsic dimensionality well below 200, and Hu et al.'s original LoRA paper found rank 4–8 sufficient for single-task adaptation of GPT-3-scale models, but compositional register is explicitly a multi-task interference problem — you are simultaneously encoding legal-syntactic and dialogue-pragmatic directions that may be nearly orthogonal in the middle-layer weight space — which argues for rank 16–32 at minimum to avoid the two register subspaces collapsing onto the same low-rank approximation. The overfitting risk from rank being too high is real but asymmetric: a rank that is too low produces the same register collapse we've been diagnosing all along (the dominant-loss register wins the low-rank approximation), while a rank that is too high overfits to the specific hybrid examples in the fine-tuning set and fails to generalize to novel compositional combinations — the practical heuristic from the QLoRA and LongLoRA literature is to use rank 32 with a strong dropout on the LoRA B matrix (0.1–0.15) as a regularizer that prevents individual rank components from specializing too tightly to training examples. Selective application to middle layers only (roughly layers 12–20 in a 32-layer model) is well-motivated by everything established earlier in this conversation, but it introduces a new risk: gradient starvation of early and late layers, which are frozen and therefore cannot adjust to the new middle-layer transformation geometry, meaning the middle-layer LoRA must simultaneously span the compositional register subspace and remain compatible with the frozen early/late layer representations it is sandwiched between — a constraint that effectively reduces the usable rank, since some rank components must be spent on compatibility rather than register expressivity. The empirically testable prediction is that selective middle-layer LoRA at rank 32 with dropout will outperform flat prefix tuning on compositional register benchmarks by a meaningful margin on coherence metrics (BERTScore, register consistency classifiers) but will show degraded performance relative to full-layer LoRA at rank 8 on tasks requiring long-range syntactic dependencies, precisely because the frozen early layers cannot adjust their syntactic feature encoding to match what the modified middle layers now expect.

Yes, there is a principled quantification, and it lives in the singular value decomposition of the LoRA update matrix after training: the singular values of ΔW = BA decompose the learned update into rank-1 components ordered by contribution magnitude, and you can partition these components into "compatibility" versus "expressivity" by projecting each singular vector onto two reference subspaces — the frozen layer's existing weight null space (directions the original weight matrix already suppresses, which LoRA must avoid corrupting) versus the register-contrast subspace (directions that maximally separate legal-formal from dialogue-informal activations, extractable via a linear probe trained on register-labeled activations before LoRA is applied). The fraction of total singular value mass that aligns with the null-space-preservation subspace is your compatibility tax — empirically, based on the spectral analysis work in AdaLoRA (Zhang et al. 2023), which dynamically allocates rank by pruning low-magnitude singular values, you would expect this tax to be highest in the layers immediately adjacent to the frozen boundary (layers 11 and 21 in a 12–20 scope), potentially consuming 40–60% of effective rank there while dropping to 15–20% in the center of the LoRA scope (layer 16), because central layers face frozen neighbors only through residual stream accumulation rather than direct attention interaction. This measurement can drive dynamic layer inclusion decisions, and the architecture for doing so already exists implicitly in AdaLoRA's importance scoring and DyLoRA (Valipour et al. 2022), which trains nested LoRA ranks simultaneously to allow post-hoc rank selection — the extension needed here is to replace their loss-gradient importance criterion with the compatibility-tax criterion, including a layer in the LoRA scope only when its register-expressivity fraction exceeds its compatibility-tax fraction, which would likely pull in some early layers (where register priors are set) and some late layers (where unembedding alignment occurs) while excluding the immediately-boundary layers that pay the highest compatibility tax for the least expressivity return. The practical procedure would be: train a full-scope LoRA at high rank (64) for a small number of steps, compute per-layer SVD decompositions, project singular vectors onto both reference subspaces, rank layers by expressivity-to-compatibility ratio, then retrain with a reduced scope containing only layers above a threshold ratio — this is a one-extra-training-run overhead, not a continuous search. The deeper theoretical point is that this reframes layer selection from a geometric heuristic (middle layers matter because of what we know about representational depth) into a data-driven spectral decision that is specific to the register pair being bridged, which means the optimal LoRA scope for legal-to-dialogue transfer could differ substantially from the optimal scope for, say, clinical-to-social-media transfer, even in the same base model — a prediction with direct practical implications for parameter-efficient fine-tuning pipelines that currently treat layer scope as a fixed architectural choice.
